idiom_name: public methods holding std::scoped_lock/std::lock_guard + private *_impl methods
implementation_notes: std::mutex offers exclusive, non-recursive ownership and the standard requires that a thread must not already own the mutex before calling lock or try_lock, so an intra-component call that locks again is undefined behaviour; the realization is to have every public method open a std::lock_guard (or std::scoped_lock for several members) and forward to a private *_impl method that touches the members directly. The precondition lives in the naming and in a comment at each definition; where the team wants it enforced, pass the guard by reference into the implementation method so a call without the lock does not compile. std::recursive_mutex exists - its reference example is literally a class whose member functions call each other - but paying for recursion to tolerate a self-call is the anti-fix the pattern is named against.
pitfalls: Re-locking std::mutex is undefined behaviour (typically a deadlock); std::recursive_mutex suppresses the symptom, adds a lock count of unspecified maximum depth, and hides the double acquisition.

Virtual calls are the trap: an *_impl method that calls a virtual function may re-enter a public method that locks, so implementation methods should stay non-virtual and call only other implementation methods.
A const public method needs a mutable mutex member; holding the guard across a callback or a blocking call turns a short critical section into a long one.
Nothing enforces the precondition unless the guard is passed into the implementation method: a plain private method can be called from anywhere inside the class.
